client: I got some news from my doctor a few weeks ago that I'm still trying to process — it turns out I have a chronic illness, and honestly, I don't even fully understand what that means for my life going forward. Ever since the diagnosis, I've just been walking around with this constant knot in my stomach, like the future I thought I had is just... gone. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I guess I'm here because I don't know what else to do.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds really heavy — receiving a diagnosis like this can shake the very ground you thought you were standing on, and that constant knot in your stomach makes complete sense given how much uncertainty you're sitting with. I'm really glad you're here, even if part of you isn't sure it will help, because just beginning to put words to this takes courage. When you say the future you thought you had feels gone, I'm curious — what does that future look like in your mind, and what feels most threatened by this news?

client: I think what I keep coming back to is this image I had of myself — still active, independent, maybe traveling more once I got older, just... living without having to think about my body all the time. Now I feel like every plan I make has this giant question mark hanging over it, like I can't trust anything I used to assume. And honestly, what scares me most is becoming a burden to the people around me, like my whole identity might just collapse into being "the sick person."
therapist: The fear of losing that version of yourself — active, independent, free — and being reduced to just a diagnosis in other people's eyes is such a painful thing to sit with, and it makes a lot of sense that this is where your mind keeps landing. I want to gently notice something though: right now, your mind seems to be jumping quite far ahead, collapsing a very uncertain future into a kind of inevitable story about burden and lost identity — and that story, as real as it feels, is still a story, not a fact. What evidence do you have, from the people around you or from who you've been so far, that your worth and your relationships depend on you *never* needing support?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I know logically that my friends and family don't actually think of me that way — but it's hard to really believe it right now, because I've always been the one who holds things together for other people, not the other way around. The idea of needing support feels almost shameful, like I'd be breaking some unspoken contract I have with the people in my life. So even if the story isn't a fact, I don't know how to just... stop believing it.
therapist: That sense of shame around needing support — like you'd be betraying a role you've built your whole identity around — is such an important thing to name, and it takes real honesty to recognize it. What you're describing sounds less like a logical belief and more like a deeply held rule you've lived by for a long time, which is exactly why it doesn't just switch off when you reason against it. I'm curious — where do you think that "unspoken contract" came from, and has there ever been a moment when someone you care about needed *you*, and you thought less of them for it?

client: No, of course not — when people I care about have gone through hard times and leaned on me, I never thought less of them. If anything, I think I felt closer to them, like they trusted me enough to let me see that side of them. But somehow that doesn't translate when I think about myself — it's like there's one rule for everyone else and a completely different, harsher one for me, and I can see the contradiction but I still can't make it feel any different.
therapist: You just did something really significant — you caught your own double standard in real time, and that kind of clarity is genuinely meaningful, even if it doesn't yet *feel* different in your body. The gap between knowing something and feeling it is real, and it's not a flaw in you — it just means this rule has had a lot of years to settle in deeply, and it will take more than one insight to loosen it. I wonder, if a close friend came to you and described themselves exactly the way you've described yourself tonight — the contradiction, the shame, the fear of being a burden — what would you want them to hear?

client: I think I'd want them to hear that needing help doesn't erase everything they've ever been, that one hard chapter doesn't rewrite the whole story. But when I try to direct that toward myself, it just feels hollow, like I'm reciting something I don't actually believe yet. I guess I understand why you're asking me to do that, but it feels a little too neat — like the answer is obvious but the feeling is still completely stuck somewhere I can't reach.
therapist: That feeling of "I know the right words but they land hollow" is actually really honest and important feedback — it means you're not just going through the motions, and it tells us that the work isn't about finding the *right phrase* but about slowly building experiences that make the belief feel true, not just sound true. You're not stuck because you're doing something wrong; you're stuck because this is genuinely hard, and insight alone rarely moves the feeling — that usually comes more gradually, through small moments that accumulate over time. I'm wondering, in your day-to-day life right now, is there any small way you've already allowed yourself to receive support — even something minor — that you might have been dismissing as insignificant?

client: Actually, my neighbor brought over food a couple of weeks ago after I mentioned I hadn't been eating well, and I remember feeling really uncomfortable accepting it — I kept saying it wasn't necessary and almost sent her away. I did take it in the end, but I spent the rest of the evening feeling guilty about it, like I'd somehow imposed on her even though she offered. I guess that's an example, but I'm not sure it counts as "allowing" myself to receive support so much as just... failing to refuse it successfully.
therapist: The way you just framed that — "failing to refuse it successfully" — is so telling, because it means even when you let something good in, your mind immediately reframes it as a defeat rather than a moment of connection. But here's what I notice: your neighbor wasn't burdened, she wasn't asked, she *chose* to show up for you — and you letting her do that wasn't an imposition, it was actually giving her the same gift you've described feeling when people trusted you enough to lean on you. I'm curious, when you imagine your neighbor's experience that evening, do you think she went home feeling imposed upon — or might she have felt something else entirely?

client: Honestly, when I actually picture her that evening, I don't think she went home feeling burdened — she's a warm person and she probably felt good about it, maybe even glad she did something useful. But there's this stubborn part of me that keeps insisting my situation is different, like I'm a special case where the normal rules don't apply and people are just being polite when they help me. I know that probably sounds irrational, but it's hard to shake the feeling that I'm somehow more of an imposition than other people would be.
therapist: That "special case" feeling is so common and so stubborn — it's like your mind has built a small exception clause just for you, where all the compassion and logic that applies to everyone else somehow doesn't quite reach. What's worth noticing is that you *can* picture your neighbor's genuine warmth, you *can* reason your way to the more likely truth — and that's not nothing, even if the stubborn part isn't fully convinced yet. I'm curious about that voice that insists you're different — if you had to guess, how long has it been telling you that, and do you think it might have once been trying to protect you from something?

client: That question actually stopped me for a second, because I think that voice has been there for a really long time — maybe since I was pretty young, when being capable and self-sufficient felt like the safest way to keep things stable around me. So yeah, I can see how it might have been protective once, like if I never needed anything, I couldn't be let down or seen as too much. But I'm not sure knowing that actually helps me feel any differently right now — it's almost like understanding where it came from makes it feel more entrenched, not less.
therapist: What you just uncovered is genuinely significant — that voice wasn't born from weakness, it was a child's very smart way of staying safe, and it makes complete sense that it's held on so tightly for so long. And I hear you that understanding its origins can feel like it locks it in rather than loosens it — but I'd gently offer that there's a difference between a strategy that once *protected* a younger version of you and one that's actually *serving* you now, in this chapter of your life. I'm wondering — that younger part of you who learned to never need anything, what do you think they most needed to hear back then that they didn't get to?

client: I think that younger version of me needed to hear that it was okay to take up space, that needing things didn't make me a burden or a problem to be managed. Just saying that out loud feels surprisingly heavy, like there's some grief attached to it that I wasn't expecting. I don't really know what to do with that feeling right now — it's a bit overwhelming and I'm not sure this is something I can just sit with comfortably on my own.
therapist: That grief makes complete sense — you just touched something real and tender that's been waiting a long time to be acknowledged, and it's okay that it feels heavy right now rather than neat or resolved. You don't have to know what to do with it in this moment; sometimes the most important thing is just to let it be there without rushing past it or pushing it away. I want to gently check in — when you say you're not sure you can sit with this comfortably on your own, do you have anyone in your life, or any support around you, that feels safe enough to be with in moments like this one?

client: There are a couple of people who probably could be that for me — my sister, maybe one close friend — but the idea of actually reaching out and saying "I'm struggling and I need you right now" feels almost impossible, like I'd have to overcome this enormous wall just to get the words out. I think part of me is afraid that if I actually let someone see how much I'm unraveling over this diagnosis, it'll make it more real somehow, like saying it out loud seals it. So even knowing the support might be there doesn't make it feel accessible, if that makes sense.
therapist: What you're describing makes complete sense — that wall isn't just about pride or the old rule about not needing things, it's also about the fear that speaking something out loud gives it a kind of permanence, and that feels like a lot to risk all at once. But I want to gently offer another way of looking at it: the unraveling is already happening inside you, whether or not you say the words — and letting someone in doesn't create the reality, it just means you don't have to carry it entirely alone anymore. I'm wondering if reaching out has to be the full, vulnerable declaration all at once, or whether there might be a smaller, more manageable first step — even just letting your sister or your friend *be near you* without having to perfectly explain everything yet?
